newsitem.title: USA: Gephardt likely to oppose China MFN status renewal.
newsitem.headline: Gephardt likely to oppose China MFN status renewal.

text.p: House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt on Sunday hinted he would oppose extending most-favored-nation (MFN) trade status to China that the Clinton administration favors.
China's MFN status and the favorable tariffs that it enjoys on its exports to the United States expires in June. Last week President Bill Clinton announced its renewal for another year.
The decision was expected to set off a fierce debate in S. Congress, which has the right to overturn Clinton's decision.

"I believe the engagement that we have constructed with China while it has many good aspects, needs to be tougher, needs to be more agressive, needs to be more forceful," Gephardt, of Missouri, said on CNN's "Late Edition with Frank Sesno."

While not stating outright that he would oppose renewing MFN status to China, he maintained that U.S. trade sanctions in the past, namely with South Africa, have helped put an end to human rights violations.
"I think that is what we have to do both for moral reasons and for trade and economic reasons," he said, adding that he would announce his intentions regarding China's trade status on Tuesday.

Rep. John Kasich, an Ohio Republican, said on "Fox News Sunday" that he would oppose MFN treatment to China. "I'm going to vote against it ... I think their actions have been absolutely unconscionable and they're getting worse," Kasich said.
Gephardt, a potential contender for the Democratic Party's presidential nomination in 2000, appears to be distancing himself from the Clinton Administration.
Last week he opposed a balanced budget measure approved by the U.S. House of Representatives.
"When it comes to the people at the top, they are getting a huge tax cut in this budget," Gephardt said. "I can't support that."

"It makes no sense whatsoever to give the top 1 percent of taxpayers, who make an average of $650,000 a year, over a $6,000 tax break per year," he said. "We now have the largest disparity between the wealthy and the middle class than we've had in this country in more than 30 years."
